title: Prevalence and Course of PTSD and Dissociative Symptoms in Obese Patients Before and After Bariatric Surgery: A Prospective Observational Study
summary: The study examines how frequently posttraumatic stress disorder and dissociative symptoms occur in people with severe obesity who are planning to undergo weight loss surgery. Since obesity is often linked to psychological distress, especially due to traumatic experiences in childhood, these mental health symptoms often affect body perception and eating behavior, which can complicate obesity treatment. The study follows participants before the surgery and up to one year afterward, using interviews and questionnaires to gather information about their mental health. The goal is to better understand the prevalence and changes in symptoms related to weight loss. The hypothesis is that these psychological burdens are more pronounced in affected individuals than in people without obesity and that they change following surgery. The insights gained are intended to help tailor future treatments more effectively to meet the specific needs of these patients and improve their care.

interventions.name: Severely obese patients who are scheduled for obesity surgery are interviewed shortly before the operation and again at a one-year follow-up. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients who, according to current guidelines for bariatric surgery, have an appropriate BMI (e.g., BMI ≥ 35 kg/m² with comorbidities or BMI ≥ 40 kg/m²) and are seeking surgery
Patients who are able to participate in clinical interviews in person (or, if applicable, by telephone/online)
Patients with internet access
Patients who are able to understand the online questionnaire and complete it independently
Exclusion criteria:
Acute psychotic or manic episode
Acute crisis situation
Acute suicidality
Current substance use
Insufficient language skills
No internet access or inability to complete online questionnaires
